lesson.title: Apples to Oranges: Using Z-Scores to Compare Across Different Scales
lesson.summary: Because z-scores strip away original units, they let you fairly compare values from entirely different distributions, answering questions that raw numbers alone cannot, such as which of two differently scaled performances was relatively stronger.
lesson.body:
The entire point of building z-scores and standardizing a distribution comes together in this final skill: using z-scores to make fair comparisons across values that started out on completely different scales. Raw numbers alone often cannot answer a question like which performance was better, if the two performances were measured on different tests, in different units, or against different groups. Z-scores solve this by converting every value into the same standardized currency: number of standard deviations from its own mean.

Suppose a student scores 650 on a test with mean 500 and standard deviation 100, giving a z-score of 1.5, exactly as calculated earlier. Now suppose that same student takes a second, differently scaled test with mean 21 and standard deviation 5, and scores 27 on it. That student's z-score on the second test is 27 minus 21, divided by 5, which is 6 divided by 5, or 1.2. Comparing the raw scores, 650 versus 27, tells you nothing useful since the tests use entirely different scales. Comparing the z-scores, 1.5 versus 1.2, tells you clearly that the student performed relatively better, in terms of standard deviations above the mean, on the first test than on the second, even though both scores were well above average.

This same logic extends to comparing two different people rather than one person's two scores. If one runner finishes a race with a z-score of negative 1.8 relative to their race's field, and another runner finishes a different race with a z-score of negative 1.2 relative to their own field, the first runner's time was more standard deviations away from that race's average, a meaningfully different statement than simply comparing raw finishing times, which would be affected by different courses, weather, and competitors.

This kind of comparison depends on everything from earlier sections working together correctly. It requires computing accurate means and standard deviations for each distribution, calculating each z-score correctly, and then interpreting the resulting z-scores with attention to both sign and magnitude, since a comparison that ignores sign, or that treats a z-score of 1.5 and negative 1.5 as similarly good, would completely misread the situation. It also inherits every caution already raised about z-scores: the comparison is most trustworthy when both distributions are reasonably free of extreme outliers and not severely skewed, since skew or outliers can distort the mean and standard deviation each z-score depends on.

Used carefully, though, comparing z-scores is one of the most practically valuable tools introduced in this unit. It is the same underlying idea used when college admissions offices compare applicants from different high schools with different grading scales, when doctors compare a child's growth measurements to age-specific norms, and when scientists compare effect sizes across different experiments measured in different units. Every one of these comparisons rests on the same principle: convert to a standardized scale first, then compare, because raw numbers on different scales are almost never directly comparable.
